No. One thing many people don't know about kibbutzim is that they are neither "sustainable" nor self-sufficient. Basically, they can operate only if the women are undereducated and never leave the compound, while many men have to earn a living outside (and their career paths are supervised by the community). And, even with that division of labor, outside workers are hired to help run the farm. No matter what, the kibbutz ends up depending heavily on the outside world while also being in a state of weird quasi-isolation. The result is untapped human potential, sub-par resource distribution, and a higher risk of systematic human errors (think underage marriage or neglect of the sick/elderly). kibbutzim are, compared to others, shining examples of communal life -- but communal life is objectively less efficient.

At the same time, I could see myself as part of an untraditional "big family" (maybe a polyamorous thing -- 8 or 10 or adults live together, some resources are pooled, and everyone helps raise the children of 2 or 3 mothers). Sharing isn't binary -- you can share all kinds of things in moderation without the loss of individuality that comes with sharing everything.
